lessons.title: The anatomy of a test
lessons.book_section: 11.1 How to Write Tests: The Anatomy of a Test Function
lessons.objective_md: Write a test function, put it in a test module, run it with `cargo test`, and read whether it passed.

screens.heading: A test is code that checks your code
screens.text_md:
So far you checked programs by running them and reading what they printed. A **test** does that checking for you, in code, every time you ask.

Most tests do three things: **set up** some data, **run** the code you want to check, and **assert** that the result is what you expect. Here `it_works` calls `add(2, 2)` and asserts the answer is `4`.

`cargo new adder --lib` writes exactly this file for you.

coming_from.c: No GoogleTest or Catch2 to set up: the test runner ships with the compiler. `#[test]` is like `TEST(Suite, Name)`, and `#[cfg(test)]` works like an `#ifdef` that is switched on only for test builds.
coming_from.go: Close to `go test`, but a test is marked with `#[test]` instead of a `TestXxx(t *testing.T)` name, and it usually lives in the same file inside `mod tests` instead of a `_test.go` file. A failed assertion panics instead of calling `t.Errorf`.
coming_from.java: `#[test]` is Rust's JUnit `@Test` or xUnit `[Fact]`. There is no test class: tests are plain functions in a `tests` module, usually in the same file as the code they check.
coming_from.js: Like Jest or Vitest, but part of the toolchain. `#[test] fn it_works()` is the `test('it works', () => …)` call, `assert_eq!(result, 4)` is `expect(result).toBe(4)`, and `cargo test` is `npm test` with nothing to configure.
coming_from.python: Like `pytest` or `unittest`, but built in: nothing to install. A `#[test]` function plays the role of a `test_` function, and `cargo test` is your `pytest`. Tests usually sit in the same file as the code, inside `mod tests`.

question.prompt_md: Which line makes `cargo test` run a function as a test?

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `#[cfg(test)]` only says "compile this in test builds". A function under it is compiled but not run unless it also has `#[test]`.
Correct. `#[test]` marks the function, and the test runner calls every marked function.
Not quite. `use super::*;` only brings the parent module's items into scope so the tests can call them.
Not quite. The module name `tests` is a convention. Functions inside it without `#[test]` are helpers that never run on their own.

screens.heading: Running `cargo test`
screens.text_md:
`cargo test` builds your crate in test mode and runs every `#[test]` function. Each test gets one line: its full path, `tests::it_works`, then `ok`.

The summary line counts what passed and failed. `ignored` and `filtered out` come up in L11.4. The second section, `Doc-tests`, checks code inside documentation comments, which you'll meet in Chapter 14; here there are none, so it runs 0 tests.

question.prompt_md: A `#[test]` function that contains no assertions at all passes, as long as it doesn't panic.

explanations.text_md: Correct. The runner only watches for panics. A test that runs to the end without panicking passes, even if it checks nothing, which is why every useful test needs an assertion.
Not quite. Assertions are just one way to panic. A test with none can't fail by assertion, so unless something else panics, it passes.

screens.heading: Forgot `use super::*;`
screens.text_md:
You'll see this error every time you forget the import. It's the module rules from Chapter 7; nothing about it is special to tests.

Notice what *didn't* happen: no test ran, so none passed or failed. A test that doesn't compile tells you nothing about the code under test. Fix the compile error first, then read the test results.

question.prompt_md: A test module forgets `use super::*;`, so its only test can't name the function it calls. What does `cargo test` report?

options.text_md: A compile error (E0425); no test runs at all.
The test runs and fails with `FAILED`.
The test is skipped and counted as `ignored`.

explanations.text_md: Correct. The test module is compiled before anything runs, and a name that isn't in scope stops the build. There are no results to read until it compiles.
Not quite. A test fails only when it runs and panics. This one never runs: the build stops first.
Not quite. `ignored` is for tests marked `#[ignore]` (L11.4). A compile error isn't turned into a skipped test.
Not quite. That's what you'd see if the function compiled but had no `#[test]`. Here the build fails, so nothing runs and there is no summary line.

summary: A test is a function marked `#[test]`; `cargo test` runs every one and reports `ok` or `FAILED` for each.
Unit tests live in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` at the bottom of the file, compiled only for `cargo test`, with `use super::*;` to reach the code above.
A test fails when it panics, for example when an assertion fails, and passes otherwise; tests run side by side, each in its own thread.
A test module that doesn't compile runs nothing: fix compile errors before reading results.

lessons.book_section: 11.1 How to Write Tests: `assert!`, `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!`, Adding Custom Failure Messages
lessons.objective_md: Check results with `assert!`, `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!`, add messages that explain failures, and choose inputs that tell correct code from likely mistakes.

screens.heading: `assert!` checks a condition
screens.text_md:
`assert!(condition)` does nothing when the condition is `true` and panics when it is `false`. That makes it a good fit for methods that return a `bool`, like `can_hold`.

To check that something is **false**, negate it with `!`, as the second test does. Testing both answers matters: a `can_hold` that always returned `true` would pass the first test alone.

screens.heading: `assert_eq!` shows both values

coming_from.c: `assert_eq!` is like GoogleTest's `ASSERT_EQ`: it stops the test at the first failure. The type needs `PartialEq` (like `operator==`) and `Debug` (to print it).
coming_from.go: Go tests compare by hand: `if got != want { t.Fatalf(...) }`. `assert_eq!(got, want)` does the comparison and the message in one line, and stops the test at once like `t.Fatalf`.
coming_from.java: JUnit's `assertEquals(expected, actual)` cares about argument order for its message. Rust calls the two sides just `left` and `right`, so either order works. Equality comes from `PartialEq`, Rust's `equals()`.
coming_from.js: `assert_eq!(result, 4)` is `expect(result).toBe(4)`. Rust has no matcher library: you use `assert!`, `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!`, plus a custom message when you need more context.
coming_from.python: `assert_eq!(a, b)` is like pytest's `assert a == b`, which also shows both sides on failure. Rust's plain `assert!` doesn't show them, so prefer `assert_eq!` for comparisons.

steps.caption_md: `add_two(2)` should give 4, but this version has a bug: it adds 3. So `result` is 5.
steps.visual_md: Variables table with one row: `result` · `u64` · `5`, row highlighted as just changed. Line 2 of the code (`a + 3`) carries a red `bug` tag.

steps.caption_md: `assert_eq!(a, b)` panics when `a != b` and prints **both** values: `left` is the first argument, `right` the second. A plain `assert!(result == 4)` would only say that it failed.
steps.visual_md: Variables table unchanged. A red failure card appears beside it reading `left: 5` and `right: 4`, with `left` pointing to `result` and `right` pointing to the literal `4`. The output panel shows the failure.

steps.caption_md: `assert_ne!(a, b)` is the opposite: it panics when the two are **equal**. Use it when you know what a value must not be. Argument order only changes which value is printed as `left`.
steps.visual_md: The failure card is replaced by a grey card reading `assert_ne!(result, 4)` → `passes when result is not 4`. The output panel stays.

question.prompt_md: A test runs `assert_eq!(add_two(2), 4);` and a buggy `add_two` returns 5. What does the failure show?

explanations.text_md: Correct. `left` is the first argument, `add_two(2)`, which is 5; `right` is the second, 4.
Not quite. The labels follow argument order, not "expected first". The first argument here is `add_two(2)`, so `left` is 5.
Not quite. That's what `assert!` prints. `assert_eq!` always prints both values.
Not quite. Rust doesn't use the words expected and actual. It prints `left` and `right`.

screens.heading: Custom failure messages
screens.text_md:
Any arguments after the required ones are passed to `format!`, so you can write a message with `{}` placeholders. Without it, this failure would only say ``assertion failed: result.contains("Carol")``.

A good message says what the check means and shows the value you actually got. Here you see at once that the name is missing. `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!` take a message the same way, after their two values.

screens.heading: A good test fails on a buggy version

steps.caption_md: Imagine three buggy versions of the function. The typical test, `[50, 70, 90]` with mark 60, catches only Bug 3. Bugs 1 and 2 still return 2, so they slip through.
steps.visual_md: Column `[50, 70, 90]` filled in: Bug 1 grey `passes (2)`, Bug 2 grey `passes (2)`, Bug 3 red `FAILS (1)`. Other columns blank.

steps.caption_md: A **boundary** test, with a score exactly equal to the mark, catches Bug 1: `>` instead of `>=`. Off-by-one mistakes live at boundaries, so test right on them.
steps.visual_md: Column `[60]` filled in: Bug 1 red `FAILS (0)`, Bug 2 red `FAILS (0)`, Bug 3 grey `passes (1)`. Column 1 stays.

steps.caption_md: The **empty** list makes Bug 2 panic: `&scores[1..]` is out of range when there are no scores. A panic in a test is a failure, so the bug is caught.
steps.visual_md: Column `[]` filled in: Bug 1 grey `passes (0)`, Bug 2 red `FAILS (panics)`, Bug 3 grey `passes (0)`. Columns 1–2 stay.

steps.caption_md: Putting the passing score **first** catches Bug 2 too: it skips index 0. Now every bug fails at least one test. That's the goal: for each likely mistake, a test that tells it apart from correct code.

question.prompt_md: The correct function is `fn is_adult(age: u32) -> bool { age >= 18 }`. A buggy version uses `age > 18`. Which test catches the bug?

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Both versions say 30 is an adult, so this test passes on the bug too.
Not quite. Both versions say 10 isn't an adult. The test can't tell them apart.
Correct. 18 is the boundary: the correct version returns `true`, the buggy one `false`, so the assertion fails on the bug.
Not quite. 0 is an edge of the `u32` range, but both versions return `false` for it.

screens.heading: A checklist for choosing test cases
screens.text_md:
Before writing tests, list the mistakes someone could make, then pick inputs that expose them:

- **Normal**: one or two typical inputs.
- **Edges**: empty input, a single item.
- **Boundaries**: exactly on a limit, one below, one above; `0` and the type's maximum.
- **Text**: non-ASCII, such as `é` or `日本`, and whitespace other than spaces.
- **Error paths**: bad input gives the `Err` or panic you promised.

Test one behaviour per test, and name the test after it, so the list of failures reads like a description of the bug. Later in this chapter, Rusticoder checks your tests the same way Screen 5 did: it runs them against versions of the code with a planted bug, and a good set of tests fails on every one.

question.prompt_md: You're testing `fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str`, which returns the text before the first space. You already have a test for `"hello world"`. Which of these inputs are edge cases worth their own test? (Select all that apply.)

explanations.text_md: Correct. Empty input is the classic edge: the function must return `""` without panicking.
Correct. With no space at all, a function that only returns text when it finds a space would get this wrong.
Not quite. This is another normal two-word case, just like `"hello world"`. It's unlikely to catch a bug the first test misses.
Correct. A space at index 0 is a boundary: the first word is empty, which off-by-one code often gets wrong.

summary: `assert!(cond)` checks a `bool`; `assert!(!cond)` checks that it is `false`.
`assert_eq!(a, b)` and `assert_ne!(a, b)` compare with `==` and `!=` and print both values as `left` and `right` on failure; the type needs `PartialEq` and `Debug`.
Arguments after the required ones are a `format!` message: say what the check means and show the value you got.
Choose cases from likely mistakes: boundaries, empty and single inputs, non-ASCII text and error paths. A good set of tests fails on every plausible bug.

lessons.title: Testing panics and returning `Result` from tests
lessons.book_section: 11.1 How to Write Tests: Checking for Panics with `should_panic`, Using `Result<T, E>` in Tests
lessons.objective_md: Test code that must panic with `#[should_panic(expected = "…")]`, and write tests that return `Result` so they can use `?`.

screens.heading: Some code is supposed to panic
screens.text_md:
`Guess::new` promises to panic for values outside 1 to 100. That promise deserves a test too.

Add `#[should_panic]` under `#[test]`. Now the test **passes if the code panics**, and fails if the function finishes normally. The runner marks such tests `- should panic`.

coming_from.c: Like GoogleTest's death tests (`EXPECT_DEATH`), but cheap: the panic is caught in the test's own thread, and the rest of the run continues.
coming_from.go: Go tests check panics with `defer` and `recover()`. Rust needs one attribute: `#[should_panic]`. For errors returned as values, you assert on the `Result`, just as you'd check `err != nil`.
coming_from.java: Like JUnit's `assertThrows` or the older `@Test(expected = …)`. Rust checks the panic message text, not an exception type, because a panic isn't a typed exception.
coming_from.js: Like `expect(() => fn()).toThrow('message')`. Rust's version is an attribute on the test: the entire test body must panic, and `expected` checks part of the panic message.
coming_from.python: `#[should_panic]` is like `with pytest.raises(...)`, and `expected = "…"` (next screens) is like its `match=` argument. In Rust the whole test body is the block that must panic.

left.label: Passes on any panic
left.caption_md: This test passes whatever the panic is, even one from an unrelated bug, such as a slice index out of range somewhere else in `new`.

right.label: Checks the message
right.caption_md: With `expected = "…"`, the test passes only if the panic message **contains** that text. A distinctive part of the message is enough.

question.prompt_md: A `#[should_panic]` test fails if the code it calls returns normally.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `#[should_panic]` flips the rule: the test passes only if something in it panics. Returning normally makes it fail with `test did not panic as expected`.
Not quite. A normal return is exactly what `#[should_panic]` treats as failure, which is how it caught the missing `> 100` check.

screens.heading: The wrong panic fails a precise test
screens.text_md:
Here the two messages were swapped by mistake. The code still panics, so a bare `#[should_panic]` would pass.

The precise test fails instead, and shows both the real panic message and the substring it expected. Now you know which branch ran.

screens.heading: Two sets of options, split by `--`
screens.text_md:
`cargo test` first builds a test binary, then runs it. Some options are for Cargo, others for that binary.

Before `--` go Cargo's options and one optional test-name filter. After `--` go the test binary's options. `cargo test --help` lists the first kind; `cargo test -- --help` lists the second.

The output below runs the four tests of Screen 4 with `cargo test add -- --test-threads=1`: the filter `add` keeps two of them, and they run one after another.

coming_from.c: Like GoogleTest's `--gtest_filter=*add*` and the `DISABLED_` prefix. Arguments after `--` go to the test binary itself, the way you'd pass flags to a GoogleTest executable.
coming_from.go: Close to `go test -run add`, `go test -v` and `t.Skip()`. Go runs tests one at a time unless they call `t.Parallel()`; Rust is the other way round: parallel unless you pass `--test-threads=1`.
coming_from.java: Filtering is like Maven's `-Dtest=…` or `dotnet test --filter`, and `#[ignore]` is JUnit's `@Disabled` or xUnit's `Skip`. Rust runs tests in parallel threads by default, which JUnit doesn't.
coming_from.js: Like `jest -t add` to filter by name and `test.skip` to skip. Jest runs the tests in one file in order; Rust runs every test in parallel, so tests must not share state.
coming_from.python: `cargo test add` is like `pytest -k add`, `-- --show-output` shows what passing tests printed (`pytest -s` is closer to `-- --nocapture`), and `#[ignore]` is like `@pytest.mark.skip`. Unlike plain pytest, Rust runs tests in parallel by default.

screens.text_md:
Give `cargo test` a name to run only matching tests. It runs every test whose **full name contains** that text, so `add` runs two tests, and the rest count as `filtered out`. The module is part of the name, `tests::one_hundred`, so a module name works as a filter too.

screens.heading: Ignoring slow tests
screens.text_md:
Mark a slow test with `#[ignore]` under `#[test]`, optionally with a reason: `#[ignore = "slow"]`. A normal `cargo test` skips it and lists it as `ignored, slow`.

When you have time, `cargo test -- --ignored` runs **only** the ignored tests (the others count as filtered out), and `cargo test -- --include-ignored` runs all of them, ignored or not. An ignored test is still compiled every time, so it can't hide a compile error.

A filter runs every test whose full name (`tests::add_two_and_two`) contains the text; the rest are `filtered out`.
`#[ignore = "reason"]` skips a test by default; `-- --ignored` runs only ignored tests and `-- --include-ignored` runs everything.
Tests run in parallel threads by default, so they must not share files or other state; `-- --test-threads=1` runs them one at a time.
Output of passing tests is captured: `-- --show-output` shows it afterwards, `-- --nocapture` prints it as it happens.

lessons.title: Unit tests and integration tests
lessons.objective_md: Put unit tests next to the code (where they may test private functions) and integration tests in `tests/` (where they use only the public API), and share helpers between test files.

screens.heading: Two kinds of tests

coming_from.c: Integration tests are like a separate test executable linked against your library: they see only the public header. Unit tests are compiled into the library's test build and can see `static` (private) functions.
coming_from.go: Unit tests are like Go's internal tests (`package foo` in `foo_test.go`), which see unexported names. Integration tests are like external tests (`package foo_test`), which see only exported ones.
coming_from.java: Java keeps tests in `src/test/java` and reaches package-private members by sharing the package. Rust's unit tests sit in the same file and see private items; integration tests in `tests/` see only `pub` items, like a separate test project.
coming_from.js: Unit tests live in the same file as the code, not in a `*.test.js` file beside it. Integration tests in `tests/` import your crate the way an npm user imports your package: only exported (`pub`) items are visible.
coming_from.python: Rust's unit tests sit inside the module file itself, unlike Python's separate `test_*.py` files. The `tests/` folder is closer to a Python test folder that imports your package from outside.

Whether you *should* test private details is a judgement call. Rust lets you, and a unit test is the only kind of test that can. It pays off when a public function hides the helper's mistakes, for example behind a cap or a default.

problems.description_md:
`clamp_byte(n)` turns an `i16` into a `u8` by clamping: negative numbers become `0`, numbers above 255 become `255`, and 0 to 255 stay as they are. (A plain `n as u8` would wrap instead: `-1 as u8` is `255` and `256 as u8` is `0`.)

Write tests that cover the three ranges and their edges: in-range values including `0` and `255`, `-1` and the most negative `i16`, and `256` and the largest `i16`. Then make every failure explain itself. `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!` take an optional message after the two values, written like `format!` (Book ch. 11.1, "Adding Custom Failure Messages"):

```rust
assert_eq!(clamp_byte(-1), 0, "-1 is just below the range and should clamp to 0");
```

`parse(text)` reads a two-field setting, `port,debug`, such as `"8080,true"`, into `Config { port, debug }`. The rules, in the order they are checked:

problems.title: Test generic stack histories
problems.description_md:
`Stack<T>` is a last-in, first-out stack for any type `T`:

| Method | Does |
|---|---|
| `new()` | an empty stack |
| `push(value)` | puts `value` on top |
| `pop()` | removes the top value and returns it, `Some(value)`; `None` when empty |
| `peek()` | borrows the top value, `Some(&value)`, without removing it; `None` when empty |
| `len()`, `is_empty()` | how many values; whether there are none |
| `clear()` | removes every value |
| `require_top()` | borrows the top value; panics with `"stack is empty"` when there is none |

Inside, a private method `top_index()` gives the position of the top value: `None` when empty, `Some(len - 1)` otherwise.

A stack is stateful: whether `pop` is right depends on what was pushed before. So tests here are **histories**: a sequence of calls with an assertion after each step, such as push 1, push 2, push 3, then pop gives 3, peek shows 2, `len` is 2. One assertion at the end can't tell which step went wrong; one after each step can.

Write unit tests that cover:

- a history of pushes and pops: values come back newest first, and `len`, `is_empty` and `peek` are right after every step;
- an empty stack: `pop` and `peek` give `None`, `len` is 0, `is_empty` is `true`;
- `clear` on a stack of several values, followed by new pushes;
- `require_top`: one test where it returns the top value, and one `#[should_panic(expected = "stack is empty")]` test on an empty stack;
- the private `top_index`: `None` when empty, `Some(2)` after three pushes;
- a payload that is not `Clone` or `Copy`: define `struct Book { title: String }` in the test module, push two, and check titles through `peek` and `pop`. Use owned text with non-ASCII letters, such as `String::from("Été")`.

`peek` returns `Option<&Book>` and `Book` has no `Debug`, so take the value out before comparing: after a push you *know* there is a top, and `.expect("a book was just pushed")` says so (Book ch. 9.3). Use assertion messages that say which step of the history failed.

problems.title: Audit a borrowed-text module
problems.description_md:
This module hands out **borrowed** text: its functions return slices of the input, not copies. Audit it with both kinds of test.

| Item | Contract |
|---|---|
| `first_word(text)` | the first word, as a slice of `text`; words are separated by any Unicode whitespace. No words: the empty slice at the very start of `text`, `&text[0..0]` |
| `longest_word(text)` | the word with the most **characters** (not bytes); the first one wins a tie. No words: `&text[..0]` |
| `normalize(text)` | a new `String`: the words joined with single spaces |
| `View::new(text)` | wraps a borrowed `&str`; `first()` is `first_word` of it and `original()` returns the whole text it was given |
| `same_location(a, b)` | supplied for your tests: `true` when two slices are the very same piece of memory, not merely equal text |
| `scalar_len(text)` | **private**: the number of characters, `text.chars().count()` |

Equal text isn't enough to prove a slice is borrowed. A version of `first_word` that returns a *copy* of the right word passes every `assert_eq!`. `same_location` tells the two apart: `same_location(first_word(text), &text[2..5])` holds only when the result points into `text` at bytes 2 to 5. (You'll see how it works in Chapter 20; here it is a supplied tool.)

Write tests in two places:

- **unit tests** in `src/lib.rs`'s `tests` module for the private `scalar_len`: `"éé"` has 2 characters and 4 bytes, `""` has 0, and `"e\u{301}"` has 2;
- **integration tests** in `tests/text_views.rs` for everything public. Use the shared fixture `common::unicode_fixture()` from the supplied `tests/common/mod.rs` (`"\u{3000}éé\tabc\u{3000}"`). Cover: the first word, and that it lies at bytes 3..7 of the input; the longest word by characters (`"abc"` beats `"éé"`); a tie (the first wins); text with no words (the empty slice at the start); `normalize` with inner runs of whitespace; and a `View` whose `first()` and `original()` point into the text it was given.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Run:      cargo test --test text_views -- --include-ignored, on the provided code
Expected: every test passes, and at least 5 tests run

Run:      the same tests on a version of first_word that returns an equal, leaked copy
Expected: at least one test fails (a same_location check)
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Write tests only: below the provided code in `src/lib.rs`, and in `tests/text_views.rs`. `tests/common/mod.rs` is read-only.
- At least 1 unit test calling `scalar_len`, and at least 5 tests in `tests/text_views.rs`, which declares `mod common;`.
- Use `same_location` at least once. No `unwrap()`.
hints: In the fixture, `\u{3000}` is 3 bytes and `é` is 2, so `"éé"` sits at bytes 3..7 and `"abc"` at bytes 8..11. `same_location(first_word(&text), &text[3..7])` checks the first word is borrowed from `text`, not copied.

"No words" has an exact answer too: `first_word("  ")` must be the empty slice at the start, so `same_location(first_word(&blank), &blank[0..0])` must hold. An empty `""` literal elsewhere in memory is equal, but not the same location.

A tie needs two words of equal length: in `"ab cd"`, `longest_word` must return the slice at bytes 0..2. For the `View`, build it from a `String` you keep, then compare `view.original()` with the whole string using `same_location`.
problems.solution_approach_md: The unit test pins `scalar_len` on multi-byte and combining text, which catches counting bytes. The integration tests use the fixture to catch splitting only on ASCII spaces and comparing bytes, check every returned slice with `same_location` against the exact range of the input (catching copies and unrelated empty strings), check that ties keep the first word (catching `>=`), check `normalize` on inner runs (catching splitting on single spaces), and check that a `View`'s `first` and `original` are the right slices of its text.
problems.idiomatic_md: When a function promises to *borrow*, equality is only half the contract; pointer identity is the other half, and it is usually checked indirectly (here with a supplied helper). Splitting tests between a private unit test and public integration tests mirrors how Rust projects work: unit tests for internal rules, integration tests for what users rely on.

- Required: the package's Rust files are exactly `src/lib.rs`, `tests/common/mod.rs` and `tests/text_views.rs`. Banned: `unwrap()`.
problems.notes_md:
`same_location` compares the address and the length of two slices; it is supplied so the tests can tell a borrowed result from an equal copy. The starter catches none of the mutants (`scalar_len("abc")` is 3 even when counting bytes) and fails rows 2, 4–13, 15 and 16. problems.title: Test a buggy library
problems.description_md:
The library `test_lab` has four small public functions. They are correct, and you will write the test suite that keeps them that way. Each part adds tests for one function, and Submit checks each part on its own: your tests must pass on the supplied code and fail on every version with a planted bug for that part. Part 4 moves to the outside and then checks the whole suite against all twelve planted bugs.

| Function | Contract |
|---|---|
| `clamp(n: i32) -> u8` | Negative numbers give 0, numbers above 255 give 255, 0 to 255 stay as they are. |
| `normalize(s: &str) -> String` | The words of `s`, split on any Unicode whitespace, joined with single spaces; no space at either end. |
| `valid(n: i32) -> i32` | Returns `n` for 1 to 100; panics with `"at least one"` below 1 and `"at most one hundred"` above 100. |
| `parse_count(s: &str) -> Result<u32, String>` | Trims `s` and parses it as a `u32` (0 to 4,294,967,295); anything else gives `Err(String::from("invalid"))`. |

**Part 1 · Clamp**

Write unit tests for `clamp` in the `tests` module of `src/lib.rs`: values that stay as they are (include an odd one), and values outside the range, one step outside and at the ends of `i32`. Give each assertion a message.

**Part 2 · Normalize**

Add unit tests for `normalize`: a run of spaces, spaces at both ends, words separated by a tab, `\u{3000}` and a line feed, and text that is only whitespace.

**Part 3 · Panics and results**

Add unit tests for `valid` and `parse_count`: `valid(1)` and `valid(100)` return their input; `valid(0)` and `valid(101)` panic with the right message, checked with `#[should_panic(expected = "…")]`. For `parse_count`, a test that returns `Result<(), String>` uses `?` on padded input and on the largest count; another compares the `Err` for letters and for a negative number.

**Part 4 · The public contract**

Write integration tests in `tests/public_contract.rs`, which uses the library as `test_lab`: at least four tests that check each function through its public API, including one `should_panic` test. Then the whole suite, unit and integration tests together, must catch all twelve planted bugs.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Run:      Part 1: cargo test -- --include-ignored, on the provided code
Expected: every test passes, and at least 2 tests run

Run:      Part 4: cargo test --test public_contract -- --include-ignored
Expected: every test passes, and at least 4 tests run
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Write tests only: below the provided code in `src/lib.rs`, and in `tests/public_contract.rs`. The provided code is read-only.
- The package's Rust files are `src/lib.rs` and `tests/public_contract.rs`. No `unwrap()`.
hints: Work one part at a time, and for each function ask: which input would a slightly wrong version get wrong? The edges of every range are the first candidates: -1 and 256, 0 and 101, 1 and 100, and `u32::MAX` for counts.
Output text is compared exactly, so test both ends of `normalize`'s result (no leading or trailing space) and whitespace other than spaces.
Part 4 repeats checks from the outside: `use test_lab::{clamp, normalize, parse_count, valid};` at the top, then plain `#[test]` functions, with no `mod tests`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Part 1 checks 0, an odd 7 and 255 unchanged, and -1, `i32::MIN`, 256 and `i32::MAX` clamped. Part 2 checks runs of spaces, both ends, a tab, U+3000 and a line feed, and blank text. Part 3 checks `valid` at 1 and 100 and both panics with `expected`, and `parse_count` with `?` on `" 42 "` and `"4294967295"` plus the exact `Err` for `"x"` and `"-1"`. Part 4 adds an integration test per function. Every planted bug changes one of these results.
problems.idiomatic_md: A test suite is a specification you can run. Unit tests next to the code pin down each function's edges; a short integration file checks that the public API, as users see it, keeps those promises. Messages and test names that state the case turn a failure into a bug report.
problems.source_checks_md:
